questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presented with fevers and a discharging wound on her right calf. She had a recent right calf fasciotomy due to a popliteal thrombus and end-stage renal disease on regular thrice-weekly conventional hemodialysis. She had no known drug allergies. On examination her temperature was 38.6°C, and there was purulent discharge from her right calf incision site. Investigations: Total white blood cell count 12,500 cells/mm3 Wound swab culture: positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) 2/2 blood cultures positive for MSSA
questions.lead_in: What would be most appropriate for thrice-weekly posthemodialysis dosing for treatment of this patient’s infection, assuming a planned duration of therapy of 4–6 weeks?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin Ceftazidime is only marginally active against MSSA and would not be appropriate. Linezolid dosing is unaffected by renal insufficiency or dialysis and should not be given just postdialysis. Oritavancin is not established for treatment of MSSA bacteremia nor for treatment courses of 4–6 weeks in length. Vancomycin has been found to be clinically inferior to beta-lactams (including cefazolin) for MSSA infection in patients with end-stage renal diseases on regular thriceweekly hemodialysis. Cefazolin postdialysis dosing has been shown to be effective for MSSA bacteremia in patients with end-stage renal disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q2

questions.question: Interpret the resistance mechanism from the antibiogram pattern.

parts.text: An isolate is resistant to imipenem and meropenem but susceptible to piperacillin and ceftazidime. What is the mechanism of resistance?
An isolate is resistant to ampicillin, cefazolin, and cefoxitin but intermediate to ceftriaxone. What is the mechanism of resistance?

parts_raw.text: Resistant to imipenem and meropenem but sensitive to piperacillin and ceftazidime. What is the mechanism of resistance?
Resistant to amp, cefazolin, and cefox but Intermediate to Ceftriaxone. What is the mechanism of resistance?

questions.model_answer:
a) Carbapenem resistance with retained activity of anti-pseudomonal penicillins/cephalosporins points to a non-enzymatic, carbapenem-selective mechanism: loss of the OprD (D2) porin channel, which carbapenems require for entry, typically in Pseudomonas aeruginosa (often combined with basal AmpC). A true carbapenemase would usually also compromise piperacillin and ceftazidime.
b) Resistance to ampicillin, cefazolin AND cefoxitin (a cephamycin) with only intermediate ceftriaxone is the signature of an AmpC beta-lactamase (chromosomal/inducible or plasmid-mediated). AmpC hydrolyzes cephamycins and is not inhibited by clavulanate, distinguishing it from an ESBL (ESBLs spare cefoxitin).

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, describe their (i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), (ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), and (iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.
questions.question_raw: For the following antibiotics, describe their i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.

parts.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

parts_raw.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

questions.model_answer: a) Ceftriaxone: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high susceptibility to AmpC hydrolysis; (iii) not recommended for invasive infection by an AmpC producer (derepressed mutants emerge on therapy). b) Cefepime: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low susceptibility (zwitterion penetrates rapidly and is less susceptible to AmpC inactivation); (iii) yes — treatment of choice for serious AmpC inducible-resistant strains. c) Piperacillin-tazobactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) high (tazobactam does not reliably inhibit AmpC, so the penicillin is hydrolysed); (iii) not recommended for invasive AmpC infection. d) Ceftazidime-avibactam: (i) weak inducer; (ii) low (avibactam inhibits class C/AmpC, restoring activity); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC producers. e) Imipenem: (i) strong inducer; (ii) low (stable to AmpC hydrolysis); (iii) yes — recommended for invasive AmpC infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The strong/weak induction hierarchy and the pip-tazo/imipenem entries rest on standard AmpC teaching (e.g. Tamma et al., IDSA AmpC guidance); Mandell explicitly supports only that cefepime is less susceptible to AmpC and is treatment of choice for AmpC strains, and that ceftazidime-avibactam's avibactam inhibits class C enzymes.

questions.question: Cefiderocol — what are the two components of this drug and what is the antibacterial mechanism of both?

parts.text: Cefiderocol — what are the two components of this drug and what is the antibacterial mechanism of both?

parts_raw.text: Cefiderocol - What are the two components of this drug and what is the antibacterial mechanism of both?

questions.model_answer: (1) Cephalosporin (β-lactam) core — same R1 side chain as ceftazidime; binds penicillin-binding proteins (chiefly PBP3) and inhibits peptidoglycan cross-linking (transpeptidation), blocking cell-wall synthesis. (2) Catechol siderophore moiety at R2 — chelates ferric iron and is actively taken into the bacterial cell by iron-transport systems (“Trojan horse” effect), delivering the cephalosporin into the periplasm and bypassing porin-loss and efflux resistance.

questions.question: Cefiderocol.

parts.text: Name the two different components and their mechanism.

parts_raw.text: 2 different components and their mechanism

questions.model_answer: (1) Cephalosporin (β-lactam) component — shares the ceftazidime R1 side chain, binds PBPs (high affinity for PBP3 in gram-negative rods) and inhibits the transpeptidation step of peptidoglycan cell-wall synthesis. (2) Catechol siderophore side chain at R2 — binds/chelates iron and is imported by bacterial iron-transport systems (“Trojan horse”), carrying the drug across the outer membrane into the periplasm and evading porin and efflux mechanisms; confers potent activity against class A, B, C and D β-lactamase producers.

cohort_answer.text: Cefiderocol (catechol-cephalosporin): Catechol side chain chelates ferric iron and is actively transported into the bacterial cell through the outer cell membrane via a bacterial iron transporter whose chief function is delivering iron nutrients to the cell wall. Cephalosporin component binds to peptidoglycan proteins (PBP-3, seen among non-fermenters), inhibiting the final stage of transpeptidation of peptidoglycan synthesis in the cell wall, inhibiting cell wall synthesis. No gram positive or anaerobic activity (similar spectrum to Ceftazidime). Dosed 2-3g every 8 hours as extended infusion, needs CrCl adjustment. Cephalosporin component has high affinity for PBP3 (structurally similar to Cefepime, pyrrolidin group on C3 side chain, greater stability against beta-lactamases); carboxy-propanoxyomino group on C7 improves transport across outer membrane. Siderophore component: chlorocatechol group at end of C3 confers siderophore activity, an iron transporter allowing transport through transporters ('Iron Trojan Horse') avoiding resistance mechanisms such as porins and efflux pumps.

questions.question: Cefepime.

parts.text: What is the antimicrobial coverage?
What side effect is specific to cefepime?
What would make you recommend adding this to your hospital's formulary?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the antimicrobial coverage?
b) What side effect is specific to cefepime?
c) What would make you recommend adding this to your hospital's formulary?

questions.model_answer: a) Widest spectrum of the cephalosporins. Gram-positive cocci: MSSA, Streptococcus pneumoniae (including most penicillin-resistant strains) and other streptococci — but NOT MRSA or enterococci. Gram-negative: most Enterobacteriaceae including Enterobacter, Citrobacter and Serratia, plus Pseudomonas aeruginosa; the zwitterion penetrates rapidly and is less susceptible to AmpC β-lactamases (~75%–80% of third-generation-resistant Enterobacteriaceae remain susceptible). No reliable activity against Stenotrophomonas, and inactivated by ESBL/carbapenemase (class A/B) enzymes. b) Neurotoxicity — encephalopathy, myoclonus and seizures (including non-convulsive status), from GABA-A inhibition; occurs mainly with high doses in renal insufficiency, and is the adverse effect most characteristically linked to cefepime. c) It is the treatment of choice for serious infections caused by AmpC inducible-resistant gram-negatives (stable to AmpC), has anti-pseudomonal activity, and unlike ceftazidime retains potency against gram-positive cocci — giving broad reliable coverage for MDR nosocomial gram-negative infections and febrile neutropenia.

cohort_answer.text: a) Gram positives incl MSSA, S. pneumo, EXCEPT MRSA/Enterococcus. Gram negatives incl Enterobacteriaceae (stable AmpC activity), Pseudomonas, sometimes Acinetobacter, EXCEPT Steno, B. cepacia. Anaerobes: some activity vs GP anaerobes, inactive vs GN anaerobes (incl B. fragilis). No atypical coverage. b) Severe neurological reactions: encephalopathy, aphasia, myoclonus, seizures, non-convulsive status epilepticus; attributed to crossing BBB and concentration-dependent GABA antagonism; predominantly in critically ill/renal impairment patients. c) Broadest spectrum cephalosporin with enhanced activity against Enterobacteriaceae incl AmpC beta-lactamases and Pseudomonas; important for MDR gram negative nosocomial infections; high intrinsic potency from rapid periplasmic space penetration.

questions.question: Gonorrhoea in the pharynx of a man who has sex with men.

parts.text: The patient is allergic to ceftriaxone with anaphylaxis; name two options with dose and route.
The isolate is resistant to cefixime but sensitive to ceftriaxone – what is the mechanism of resistance?

parts_raw.text: Patient is allergic to ceftriaxone with anaphylaxis, name two options with dose and route.
Resistant to cefixime but sensitive to ceftriaxone – what is the mechanism of resistance.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Azithromycin 2 g PO single dose PLUS gentamicin 240 mg IM single dose. (2) Azithromycin 2 g PO single dose PLUS gemifloxacin 320 mg PO single dose. (Pharyngeal cure data for these dual regimens are limited; test of cure at 14 days.)
b) Chromosomal penA alteration of PBP2 raises the cefixime MIC; ceftriaxone stays active because ceftriaxone resistance requires additional mutations (efflux via mtr and β-lactamase are related β-lactam mechanisms).

cohort_answer.text: Two options: Azithro 2g po x1 dose + gentamicin 240mg IM x1 dose; Doxy 100mg bid po x7 days + gentamicin 240mg IM x1 dose; Azithromycin 2g po x1 dose + cipro 500mg po x1 dose. Mechanism of resistance: Point mutation on PBP2a for cefixime, multiple mutations for ceftriaxone resistance; Efflux (mtr gene), beta lactamase (TEM)

questions.question: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is cefoxitin disk resistant.
questions.question_raw: Staph aureus with cefoxitin disk R.

parts.text: To what drug does this predict resistance?
What is the most likely gene involved and gene product causing resistance? Explain the mode of resistance.

parts_raw.text: To what drug does this predict resistance?
What is the most likely gene involved and gene product causing resistance? Explain mode of resistance.

questions.model_answer: a) Oxacillin/methicillin resistance (i.e. it identifies MRSA), and by extension all beta-lactams including cephalosporins (except the anti-MRSA cephalosporins). b) Gene: mecA. Gene product: an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a (PBP2'), which has very low affinity for beta-lactams. Mode of resistance: target-site alteration - PBP2a substitutes for the native PBPs and continues cell-wall transpeptidation despite beta-lactam concentrations that inactivate the normal PBPs, so cell-wall synthesis proceeds.

cohort_answer.text: Predicts resistance to: Methicillin resistance - oxacillin, cefazolin, cephalexin. Gene: mecA gene - encodes PBP2a that has a low affinity for beta lactam abx. Mode of resistance: Target site alteration

questions.question_raw: Name the molecular target of each antifungal drug in the table.

parts.text: Posaconazole
Micafungin
Amphotericin
Terbinafine

parts_raw.text: Posaconazole
Micafungin
Amphotericin
Terbinafine

questions.model_answer: a) Posaconazole: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (Erg11/CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol. b) Micafungin: 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (fungal cell wall synthesis). c) Amphotericin: ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane — the polyene binds ergosterol, forming pores that increase membrane permeability. d) Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase (squalene monooxygenase), an early step in ergosterol biosynthesis.

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam.

parts.text: Name 3 mechanisms of resistance possessed by Pseudomonas aeruginosa that this antibiotic bypasses.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 mechanisms of resistance possessed by P. aeruginosa that this antibiotic bypasses

questions.model_answer: (1) Porin (OprD) loss/mutation — ceftolozane activity is unaffected by loss of the OprD outer-membrane porin. (2) Efflux pump activity — activity is unaffected by upregulated efflux systems. (3) AmpC β-lactamase — the large R2 pyrazole moiety particularly inhibits/withstands AmpC cephalosporinases, and tazobactam further inhibits class A and C enzymes.

cohort_answer.text: Efflux pumps (MexAB-OprD); Porin mutations (OprD); Modification of PBPs (ceftolozane potent inhibitor of PBP1b and 3); overexpression of AmpC (affinity for PBP4 not significant enough to induce AmpC); Class A and C beta-lactamases (tazobactam inhibits). Not effective against MBL, KPC, or OXA-48 carbapenemases

questions.question: Ceftolozane-tazobactam and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

parts.text: Name three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.

parts_raw.text: Name three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would still render the isolate susceptible to ceftolazane/tazobactam.

questions.model_answer: (1) Loss of the OprD porin channel. (2) Upregulation of RND efflux pumps (MexAB-OprM, MexXY-OprM). (3) AmpC cephalosporinase (and many ESBLs, inhibited by tazobactam). Ceftolozane's high PBP affinity and stability leave it active against these, so >80% of ceftazidime/meropenem-resistant isolates stay susceptible; it does NOT overcome metallo-β-lactamases or KPC.

questions.model_answer:
a) Caspofungin over fluconazole - azoles inhibit CYP3A4 and interact with carbamazepine (altered levels/toxicity), whereas the echinocandin has minimal CYP interaction.
b) Atovaquone over dapsone - dapsone causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
c) Doxycycline over clindamycin - clindamycin is strongly associated with C. difficile, while doxycycline is neither a C. difficile therapy nor a notable inducer of it. (Metronidazole is a C. difficile treatment, so it does not fit "not used for treatment.")
d) Levofloxacin over moxifloxacin - levofloxacin is renally excreted with high urinary concentrations, whereas moxifloxacin achieves poor urinary levels.
e) Valganciclovir over acyclovir - ganciclovir/valganciclovir is active against CMV; acyclovir is not reliably.
f) Ceftriaxone over cefuroxime - ceftriaxone reliably penetrates the CNS and is a standard meningitis agent, whereas cefuroxime has been associated with delayed CSF sterilization/meningitis failures.

questions.question: AmpC beta-lactamase production among Enterobacterales.

parts.text: Name the three species from the Enterobacterales family with the highest risk of clinically important AmpC production.

For each of the following, indicate whether it is a strong or weak inducer of AmpC (strong/weak), its risk for hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), and whether it is recommended for invasive infections (yes/no): Ceftriaxone, Cefepime, Piperacillin-tazobactam, Ceftazidime-avibactam, Imipenem.

parts_raw.text: Name the 3 species from the Enterobacterales family that has the highest risk of clinically important ampC production

For each of the following, indicate if it is a strong or weak inducer of ampC (strong/weak), risk for hydrolysis by ampC (high/low), and if it is recommended for invasive infections (yes/no): Ceftriaxone, Cefepime, Pip-Tazo, Ceftaz-Avi, Imipenem

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Enterobacter cloacae; (2) Klebsiella aerogenes (formerly Enterobacter aerogenes); (3) Citrobacter freundii. b) Ceftriaxone: weak inducer, high hydrolysis risk, not recommended. Cefepime: weak inducer, low hydrolysis risk (stable to AmpC; use when MIC <=2), recommended. Piperacillin-tazobactam: weak inducer, high hydrolysis risk, not recommended for invasive infection. Ceftazidime-avibactam: weak inducer, low hydrolysis risk, active but not first-line/routinely recommended (reserve; limited data). Imipenem: strong inducer, low hydrolysis risk (carbapenem-stable), recommended.
questions.beyond_mandell: The three high-risk AmpC species and the drug-by-drug inducer/hydrolysis/recommendation table follow IDSA guidance on AmpC-producing Enterobacterales (Tamma et al., IDSA AMR guidance); Mandell supports inducible chromosomal AmpC in Enterobacter/Klebsiella aerogenes, Citrobacter freundii and Serratia and preference for cefepime or carbapenems, but not the itemized table.

cohort_answer.text: 3 species: Enterobacter cloacae; Citrobacter freundii; Klebsiella aerogenes. Table - Ceftriaxone: Weak inducer, High hydrolysis risk, Not recommended. Cefepime: Weak inducer, Low hydrolysis risk (MIC<2), Recommended (MIC<4). Tazocin: Weak inducer, High hydrolysis risk, Not recommended. Ceftaz-Avi: Weak inducer, Low hydrolysis risk, Not recommended (limited data, for complicated UTI/intra-abdominal infections only). Imipenem: Strong inducer, Low hydrolysis risk, Recommended

questions.question: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?
questions.question_raw: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

parts.text: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam?

parts_raw.text: What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Loss/mutation of the OprD porin channel - ceftolozane-tazobactam is unaffected by loss of porin channels. (2) Upregulation of the MexAB-OprM efflux system - ceftolozane-tazobactam is unaffected by efflux pump upregulation. (3) Upregulation of the MexXY-OprM efflux system - likewise does not compromise ceftolozane-tazobactam. (Over 80% of ceftazidime- or meropenem-resistant isolates remain susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam.)

cohort_answer.text: Unaffected by porin channels (Mandell); unaffected by upregulation of efflux pumps (Mandell); MexXY efflux system (exports fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam agents); Enzymes: TEM-1, SHV-1, CTX-M, AmpC or ESBL (chromosomal beta lactamases); Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes (reduce susceptibility to all AG).
